decks.title: Biomolecules — Part 1: Carbohydrates
goals: Classify carbohydrates as monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides, and as reducing or non-reducing sugars
Describe the preparation and open-chain structure of glucose and the evidence for it
Explain the cyclic structures of glucose and fructose and the idea of anomers
Describe sucrose, maltose, lactose, starch, cellulose and glycogen and the importance of carbohydrates

slides.heading: Biomolecules
slides.body_md: Part 1 — carbohydrates: the sugars and starches that fuel living things.

headers: Example in your body or food
rows: Rice starch, cane sugar, glycogen in liver
Vitamin C in amla and citrus fruits

visual.alt: Table of the main classes of biomolecules with examples

slides.narration: Namaste! Living things are built from a few kinds of large molecules: carbohydrates, proteins, nucleic acids and lipids, helped by vitamins and hormones. The rice and roti we eat are mostly carbohydrate. In this part we study carbohydrates: how they are classified, the structure of glucose, and the sugars and starches made by joining glucose units together.

slides.heading: Classifying carbohydrates
slides.body_md: Carbohydrates are **polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones**, or compounds that give them on hydrolysis. **Monosaccharides** cannot be hydrolysed further; **oligosaccharides** give 2–10 monosaccharide units; **polysaccharides** give many. Sugars that reduce Tollens’ or Fehling’s reagent are **reducing sugars**.

visual.alt: Table classifying carbohydrates with examples, hydrolysis products and whether they are reducing

slides.narration: Carbohydrates are compounds with several hydroxyl groups and an aldehyde or ketone group, or compounds that give these on hydrolysis. Simple sugars like glucose and fructose cannot be broken into smaller sugars. Two units joined together make a disaccharide such as cane sugar, and long chains make polysaccharides like starch. Sugars with a free aldehyde or ketone group reduce Tollens’ and Fehling’s reagents.

slides.heading: Aldoses and ketoses
slides.body_md: Monosaccharides are named by the carbonyl group and the number of carbons: an **aldohexose** has an aldehyde group and six carbons (glucose); a **ketohexose** has a ketone group and six carbons (fructose).

visual.alt: Table of aldoses and ketoses with three, five and six carbon atoms and examples

slides.narration: Simple sugars are named by two features: whether they carry an aldehyde or a ketone group, and how many carbon atoms they have. So glucose, with an aldehyde group and six carbons, is an aldohexose, and fructose, with a ketone group and six carbons, is a ketohexose. Ribose in RNA is an aldopentose, with five carbons.

slides.heading: Preparing glucose
slides.body_md: Glucose is made by boiling **sucrose** with dilute acid (giving glucose and fructose), or commercially by hydrolysing **starch** with dilute H₂SO₄ at 393 K under pressure.

visual.alt: Flow showing glucose made from sucrose by acid hydrolysis and from starch by acid hydrolysis under pressure

slides.narration: Glucose occurs free in grapes and honey, but it is made by breaking down larger carbohydrates. Boiling cane sugar with dilute acid splits it into glucose and fructose. Industry hydrolyses starch from maize or potatoes with dilute sulfuric acid at about three hundred and ninety three kelvin under pressure.

slides.heading: The open-chain structure of glucose

slides.narration: In its open-chain form, glucose has six carbon atoms in a row. Carbon one is an aldehyde group. Carbons two to five each carry a hydroxyl group, and carbon six is a CH two OH group. The letter D tells us that the hydroxyl on carbon five, the lowest chiral carbon, points to the right. The plus sign often written with it tells us that glucose rotates polarised light to the right.

slides.heading: Evidence for the open-chain structure
slides.body_md: Reactions of glucose reveal its structure.

rows: Six carbons in a straight chain
An aldehyde group (oxidised, no C lost)

visual.alt: Table of reactions of glucose, their products and what each shows about its structure

slides.narration: Chemists worked out glucose’s structure from its reactions. With hydrogen iodide it gives n-hexane, so the six carbons are in a straight chain. It forms an oxime and a cyanohydrin, so it has a carbonyl group. Mild oxidation by bromine water gives gluconic acid with the same six carbons, so the carbonyl is an aldehyde. Acetylation adds five acetyl groups, so there are five hydroxyl groups, and nitric acid oxidises the end CH two OH group too.

slides.heading: Worked example: interpreting glucose reactions
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Explain what each observation tells us: (a) glucose gives a pentaacetate with ethanoic anhydride; (b) bromine water oxidises glucose to gluconic acid, $\ce{C6H12O7}$; (c) nitric acid gives saccharic acid, a dicarboxylic acid with six carbons.

**(a)** Five –OH groups, on different carbons (the compound is stable).

**(b)** The carbonyl group is an aldehyde (–CHO → –COOH with no loss of carbon).

**(c)** There is a primary alcohol group (–CH₂OH) at the other end, also oxidised to –COOH.

nodes.label: COOH (saccharic acid, with C1 also COOH)

visual.alt: Flow showing bromine water oxidising only the aldehyde end and nitric acid oxidising both ends of glucose

slides.narration: Each reaction answers one question. Five acetyl groups mean five hydroxyl groups. Bromine water is a mild oxidant that only attacks aldehydes, so getting an acid with the same carbon count proves an aldehyde group. Nitric acid is stronger and also oxidises the primary alcohol group at carbon six, giving an acid group at each end of the chain.

slides.narration: Quick check. Ask which group in glucose each reagent attacks.

slides.heading: The cyclic structure of glucose
slides.body_md: Some facts do **not** fit the open chain: glucose gives **no Schiff’s test** and no NaHSO₃ adduct, and its pentaacetate does not react with NH₂OH. Glucose exists mainly as a **six-membered ring** (pyranose) formed when the C5 –OH adds to the C1 aldehyde (a **hemiacetal**). This creates two forms, **α** and **β**, differing only at C1: they are **anomers**.

rows: Same side as ring O–C5 in Fischer projection (down in Haworth)
Both, with a trace of open chain

visual.alt: Table comparing alpha and beta D-glucose by position of the C1 hydroxyl, melting point and specific rotation, and their equilibrium in water

slides.narration: The open-chain structure cannot explain everything. Glucose does not give some typical aldehyde tests, and its pentaacetate has no free aldehyde group. The answer is that the hydroxyl group on carbon five adds to the aldehyde group, closing a six-membered ring. The new hydroxyl on carbon one can point either way, giving alpha and beta glucose, called anomers. In water they slowly interconvert, a change in rotation called mutarotation.

slides.heading: Fructose
slides.body_md: **Fructose**, C₆H₁₂O₆, is a **ketohexose** (C=O at C2), **laevorotatory** (D-(−)-fructose). It forms a five-membered ring (**furanose**) by addition of the C5 –OH to the C2 ketone group. It is a reducing sugar and is the sweetest natural sugar.

visual.alt: Table comparing glucose and fructose by type, carbonyl position, ring size, rotation and reducing power

slides.narration: Fructose has the same formula as glucose, but its carbonyl group is a ketone at carbon two. In solution it closes a five-membered ring rather than a six-membered one. It rotates plane-polarised light to the left, so it is called laevulose, and it is the sweetest of the natural sugars, found in fruit and honey. It still reduces Fehling’s solution.

slides.heading: Disaccharides
slides.body_md: Two monosaccharides join by a **glycosidic linkage** (an ether link, with loss of water). Whether the disaccharide is **reducing** depends on whether a free hemiacetal group remains.

visual.alt: Table of sucrose, maltose and lactose with their units, glycosidic linkages, reducing power and sources

slides.narration: When two sugar units join, they lose a water molecule and form a glycosidic linkage. In sucrose, the link joins carbon one of glucose to carbon two of fructose, using up both reducing groups, so sucrose is a non-reducing sugar. In maltose and lactose, the link leaves one sugar unit with a free hemiacetal group, so they are reducing sugars. Lactose is the sugar of milk.

slides.heading: Invert sugar
slides.body_md: Sucrose is **dextrorotatory** (+66.5°). On hydrolysis it gives equal amounts of glucose (+52.5°) and fructose (−92.4°); the mixture is **laevorotatory**, so the sign of rotation is **inverted** — the product is called **invert sugar**.

visual.alt: Table of specific rotations of sucrose, glucose, fructose and invert sugar

slides.narration: Cane sugar turns polarised light to the right. When it is hydrolysed, the glucose formed turns light to the right, but the fructose turns it to the left more strongly. So the mixture turns light to the left: the direction of rotation has been inverted. That is why the product is called invert sugar; it is what makes honey and many syrups stay smooth.

slides.heading: Worked example: why sucrose is non-reducing
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Sucrose does not reduce Fehling’s solution, but after boiling with dilute HCl the solution does. Explain.

**Step 1.** In sucrose, C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose — both reducing (hemiacetal or hemiketal) carbons — are used in the glycosidic bond, so no free carbonyl is available.

**Step 2.** Acid hydrolysis breaks the glycosidic bond: $\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O -> C6H12O6 + C6H12O6}$.

**Step 3.** Free glucose and fructose are reducing sugars, so Fehling’s test is now positive.

visual.alt: Flow explaining why sucrose becomes reducing after acid hydrolysis

slides.narration: Sucrose cannot reduce Fehling’s solution because its two reducing carbons are locked together in the glycosidic link. Boiling with acid breaks that link and releases glucose and fructose, each with a group that can open to a carbonyl. So after hydrolysis the solution gives a red precipitate with Fehling’s solution.

slides.heading: Quick check: reducing sugars
slides.body_md: Identify which sugar is non-reducing.
slides.narration: Quick check. Look for the sugar in which both reducing carbons are used in the glycosidic bond.

slides.heading: Polysaccharides
slides.body_md: **Starch** (plants’ store): **amylose** (15–20%, unbranched α-1,4 chains, water-soluble, blue with iodine) and **amylopectin** (80–85%, α-1,4 chains branched by α-1,6 links). **Cellulose** (plant cell walls): unbranched chains of **β**-glucose (β-1,4); humans cannot digest it. **Glycogen** (animal starch): like amylopectin but more highly branched, stored in liver and muscle.

visual.alt: Table of amylose, amylopectin, cellulose and glycogen with monomer, linkage, branching and role

slides.narration: Polysaccharides are long chains of glucose units. Starch, the energy store of plants, is a mixture of unbranched amylose and branched amylopectin, both made of alpha glucose. Cellulose, which makes plant cell walls and cotton, is built from beta glucose; our digestive enzymes cannot break those beta links, so cellulose is roughage for us. Animals store glucose as glycogen, which is even more branched than amylopectin.

slides.heading: Worked example: counting glucose units
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A sample of amylose has a molar mass of $81000\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. Estimate the number of glucose units, given that each unit in the chain is $\ce{C6H10O5}$ ($M = 162$).

**Step 1.** Each glucose joined into the chain has lost one $\ce{H2O}$: $180 - 18 = 162$.

**Step 2.** Number of units $= \dfrac{81000}{162} = 500$.

visual.alt: Table of glucose molar mass, chain-unit mass and number of units in the amylose sample

slides.narration: When glucose molecules join, each link releases a water molecule, so each unit in the chain has a mass of one hundred and sixty two, not one hundred and eighty. Dividing the chain’s molar mass, eighty one thousand, by one hundred and sixty two gives about five hundred glucose units. Real starch chains are often much longer.

slides.heading: Quick check: polysaccharides
slides.body_md: Distinguish starch, cellulose and glycogen by their linkages and branching.
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall which polysaccharide is made of beta glucose and which one is stored in animals.

Glucose: aldohexose; open chain shown by HI, NH₂OH, Br₂ water, acetylation and HNO₃ reactions.
Cyclic (pyranose) structure with α and β anomers; mutarotation.
Fructose: ketohexose, furanose, laevorotatory.
Sucrose (non-reducing, invert sugar), maltose and lactose (reducing).
Starch (amylose + amylopectin), cellulose (β-1,4), glycogen (highly branched).

visual.alt: Summary table of reducing and non-reducing carbohydrates

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones. Glucose is an aldohexose whose structure was deduced from its reactions; it exists mainly as alpha and beta rings. Fructose is a ketohexose. Sucrose is non-reducing and gives invert sugar, while maltose and lactose are reducing. Starch and glycogen store energy, and cellulose builds plant cell walls.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Know which reaction proves which feature of glucose (HI → straight chain; Br₂ water → aldehyde).
Anomers differ only at C1; they are not enantiomers.
Sucrose is non-reducing because both anomeric carbons are in the glycosidic bond.
Cellulose is β-1,4; starch and glycogen are α-linked.
Each glucose unit in a polysaccharide has mass 162 (glucose − water).

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some exam tips. Learn which reaction of glucose proves which part of its structure. Anomers differ only at carbon one. Explain the non-reducing nature of sucrose with the glycosidic bond. Remember that cellulose is made of beta glucose. And in calculations, use one hundred and sixty two for each glucose unit in a chain.

decks.title: Biomolecules — Part 2: Proteins, enzymes, vitamins, nucleic acids and hormones
goals: Describe amino acids, the peptide bond and the four levels of protein structure, and explain denaturation
Classify vitamins as fat- or water-soluble and link deficiencies to diseases
Distinguish DNA and RNA in structure and function, and state the roles of important hormones

slides.heading: Proteins and other biomolecules
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the molecules that build, run, inherit and signal in living cells.

visual.alt: Flow linking amino acids, proteins, enzymes, nucleic acids, vitamins and hormones

slides.narration: In Part 2 we meet the molecules that do most of the work in a cell. Proteins are long chains of amino acids; some are structural, like keratin in hair, and many are enzymes that speed up reactions. Nucleic acids, DNA and RNA, store and use the genetic instructions for making proteins. Vitamins and hormones, needed in small amounts, keep the whole system running.

slides.heading: Amino acids
slides.body_md: α-Amino acids have –NH₂ and –COOH on the same carbon, with a side chain R. Of about 20 in proteins, those the body cannot make are **essential** (must be in food). In water they exist as **zwitterions** (H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻), so they are crystalline, water-soluble and high-melting, and amphoteric.

rows: Only one that is not optically active

visual.alt: Table of five amino acids with their side chains and notes

slides.narration: Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins. Each has an amino group and a carboxyl group on the same carbon, plus a side chain that makes it unique. In water, the acidic group gives its proton to the basic group, forming a zwitterion with both a positive and a negative charge. That is why amino acids are crystalline solids that dissolve in water and melt at high temperatures. The ones our bodies cannot make are called essential.

slides.heading: The peptide bond
slides.body_md: The –COOH of one amino acid and the –NH₂ of another condense with loss of water, forming a **peptide bond** (–CO–NH–, an amide link). Two amino acids give a dipeptide; many give a **polypeptide**; a protein has more than about 100 residues.

slides.narration: Amino acids join through peptide bonds. The carboxyl group of one amino acid reacts with the amino group of the next, losing a molecule of water, and the resulting amide link is called a peptide bond. A chain of two amino acids is a dipeptide; a long chain is a polypeptide. Proteins are polypeptides with more than about a hundred amino acids.

slides.heading: Levels of protein structure
slides.body_md: **Primary:** the sequence of amino acids. **Secondary:** regular folding held by hydrogen bonds — **α-helix** or **β-pleated sheet**. **Tertiary:** overall folding of the chain (hydrogen bonds, disulfide links, van der Waals and ionic attractions). **Quaternary:** arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits.

rows: Hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H
H-bonds, S–S bonds, ionic and van der Waals forces

visual.alt: Table of the four levels of protein structure with descriptions and the forces holding each

slides.narration: A protein’s shape is described at four levels. The primary structure is simply the order of amino acids; changing one can change the protein’s function, as in sickle-cell anaemia. Hydrogen bonds fold the chain into helices or sheets, the secondary structure. The whole chain then folds into a compact three-dimensional shape, the tertiary structure. Some proteins, like haemoglobin, are made of several chains packed together: the quaternary structure.

slides.heading: Fibrous and globular proteins; denaturation
slides.body_md: **Fibrous** proteins have parallel chains held by H-bonds and S–S bonds; insoluble (keratin, myosin). **Globular** proteins are folded into spheres; soluble (insulin, albumin, enzymes). **Denaturation** by heat or pH change disrupts secondary and tertiary structure (but not primary), destroying biological activity.

rows: Milk curdles into paneer with lemon juice
Breaking and re-forming S–S and H-bonds

visual.alt: Table of everyday examples of protein denaturation and their causes

slides.narration: Fibrous proteins, like keratin in hair and nails, have long parallel chains and do not dissolve in water. Globular proteins, like insulin and egg albumin, are folded into compact shapes and are usually soluble. Heat or a change in pH can unfold a protein: boiling turns egg white solid, and lemon juice curdles milk to make paneer. This denaturation destroys the protein’s natural shape and activity, though the amino acid sequence is unchanged.

slides.body_md: Identify which level of protein structure survives denaturation.
slides.narration: Quick check. Denaturation breaks weak attractions, not covalent peptide bonds. Which level is defined by peptide bonds alone?

slides.heading: Enzymes
slides.body_md: Enzymes are mostly **globular proteins** that act as **biocatalysts**. They are highly **specific**, work under mild conditions (body temperature, near-neutral pH) and greatly **lower the activation energy**. Many are named with **-ase**.

visual.alt: Table of enzymes and the reactions they catalyse

slides.narration: Enzymes are nature’s catalysts. Almost all are globular proteins, and each speeds up a particular reaction, often by millions of times, at body temperature. For example, invertase splits sucrose, amylase in saliva begins breaking down starch, and pepsin in the stomach breaks down proteins. They work by lowering the activation energy, as we saw in chemical kinetics.

slides.heading: Vitamins
slides.body_md: Vitamins are organic compounds needed in **small amounts** for normal health. **Fat-soluble:** A, D, E, K (stored in liver and fat tissue). **Water-soluble:** B group and C (not stored; must be taken regularly). Vitamin B₁₂ is the exception among water-soluble vitamins: it is stored in the liver.

rows: Sunlight on skin, fish, egg yolk
Fragile red blood cells, muscular weakness

visual.alt: Table of vitamins with their deficiency diseases and sources

slides.narration: Vitamins are needed only in small amounts, but lacking them causes disease. Vitamins A, D, E and K dissolve in fat and are stored in the body. The B vitamins and vitamin C dissolve in water and are washed out in urine, so we need them regularly; vitamin C is also destroyed by cooking. Night blindness, beriberi, scurvy and rickets are classic deficiency diseases, still seen where diets are poor.

slides.heading: Worked example: linking deficiency to diet
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Suggest the vitamin involved in each case: (a) a sailor on a long voyage without fresh fruit develops bleeding gums; (b) a child kept indoors with little milk develops soft, bent leg bones; (c) a patient takes a long course of antibiotics and has cuts that keep bleeding.

**(a)** Vitamin C — scurvy.

**(b)** Vitamin D — rickets (little sunlight, little dietary vitamin D and calcium).

**(c)** Vitamin K — partly made by gut bacteria, which antibiotics reduce; deficiency increases clotting time.

visual.alt: Table linking three cases to vitamins and diseases

slides.narration: Work from the symptom and the situation. Bleeding gums after months without fresh fruit point to scurvy, a lack of vitamin C. Soft, bent bones in a child who rarely goes out in the sun point to rickets, a lack of vitamin D. And because bacteria in our gut make some vitamin K, a long course of antibiotics can lower it and slow blood clotting.

slides.heading: Quick check: vitamins
slides.body_md: Match a vitamin with its solubility or deficiency disease.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember the four fat-soluble vitamins and the diseases caused by lack of B one, C and D.

slides.heading: Nucleic acids: building blocks
slides.body_md: Nucleic acids are polymers of **nucleotides**. A **nucleoside** = nitrogenous base + pentose sugar; a **nucleotide** = nucleoside + phosphate. Nucleotides are joined by **phosphodiester** links between C5′ of one sugar and C3′ of the next.

visual.alt: Table comparing the sugar, bases and number of strands in DNA and RNA

slides.narration: Nucleic acids are long chains of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has three parts: a nitrogen-containing base, a five-carbon sugar and a phosphate group. The sugar of one nucleotide is joined to the phosphate of the next, forming a backbone. DNA uses the sugar deoxyribose and the bases adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine; RNA uses ribose and has uracil instead of thymine.

slides.heading: The DNA double helix
slides.body_md: DNA is a **double helix** of two antiparallel strands. Bases pair by **hydrogen bonds**: **A with T** (two) and **G with C** (three), so the strands are **complementary**. In any DNA, amount of A = T and G = C.

slides.narration: In DNA, two strands wind round each other in a double helix, running in opposite directions. The bases point inwards and pair up: adenine always with thymine, held by two hydrogen bonds, and guanine always with cytosine, held by three. So the order of bases on one strand fixes the order on the other. This is how DNA can be copied exactly when a cell divides.

slides.heading: Functions of nucleic acids
slides.body_md: **DNA** carries hereditary information and **replicates** itself before cell division. **RNA** helps make proteins: **mRNA** carries the message, **tRNA** brings amino acids and **rRNA** forms ribosomes. The sequence of bases (codons) decides the sequence of amino acids in a protein.

visual.alt: Flow from DNA through messenger RNA and ribosomes with transfer RNA to protein

slides.narration: DNA is the cell’s instruction book. Before a cell divides, DNA makes an exact copy of itself, so each new cell gets the full set of instructions. To make a protein, the relevant part of DNA is copied into messenger RNA, which travels to a ribosome. There, transfer RNA molecules bring the right amino acids in the order set by the code, and they are joined into a protein.

slides.heading: Worked example: base composition
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 30% adenine. What are the percentages of thymine, guanine and cytosine?

**Step 1.** A pairs with T, so T $= 30\%$.

**Step 2.** A + T $= 30 + 30 = 60\%$, so G + C $= 100 - 60 = 40\%$.

**Step 3.** G = C, so each $= \dfrac{40}{2} = 20\%$.

visual.alt: Table of base percentages in the DNA sample

slides.narration: Because adenine always pairs with thymine, they must be present in equal amounts, so thymine is also thirty percent. Together they make sixty percent, leaving forty percent for guanine and cytosine. These also pair one to one, so each is twenty percent. This equality of paired bases was one of the clues to the double-helix structure.

slides.heading: Hormones
slides.body_md: Hormones are chemical messengers made by **endocrine glands** and carried in blood. Chemically they may be **steroids** (oestrogen, testosterone, cortisol), **polypeptides** (insulin, glucagon) or **amino acid derivatives** (adrenaline, thyroxine).

rows: Controls metabolic rate; lack causes goitre/hypothyroidism

visual.alt: Table of hormones with their glands and main roles

slides.narration: Hormones carry messages between organs through the blood. Insulin and glucagon from the pancreas work in opposite directions to keep blood sugar steady. Thyroxine from the thyroid sets the rate of metabolism; iodine is needed to make it. Adrenaline prepares the body for emergencies. Steroid hormones such as testosterone and oestrogen control sexual development.

Vitamins: fat-soluble A, D, E, K; water-soluble B, C; deficiency diseases.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Proteins are chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, folded at four levels, and denatured by heat or pH. Enzymes are protein catalysts. Vitamins are needed in small amounts, and their lack causes specific diseases. DNA and RNA are chains of nucleotides that store and use genetic information, and hormones carry chemical messages around the body.

sections.heading: 1. Carbohydrates: classification and glucose
sections.body_md:
**Carbohydrates** are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones, or compounds that give these on hydrolysis.
- **Monosaccharides** (no further hydrolysis): glucose, fructose, ribose. Named by carbonyl type and carbon count — glucose is an **aldohexose**, fructose a **ketohexose**.
- **Oligosaccharides** (2–10 units): sucrose, maltose, lactose. **Polysaccharides**: starch, cellulose, glycogen.
- **Reducing sugars** reduce Tollens’ and Fehling’s reagents (free aldehyde or ketone group available): all monosaccharides, maltose, lactose. Sucrose is **non-reducing**.

**Preparing glucose:** boil sucrose with dilute acid, $\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O ->[H+] C6H12O6 + C6H12O6}$ (glucose + fructose); commercially, hydrolyse starch with dilute H₂SO₄ at 393 K under pressure.

**Open-chain structure — evidence:** HI (prolonged heating) → n-hexane (straight chain of six C); NH₂OH → oxime and HCN → cyanohydrin (C=O); bromine water → gluconic acid (the C=O is an aldehyde); ethanoic anhydride → pentaacetate (five –OH); HNO₃ → saccharic acid (primary –OH at C6). The –OH on C5 is on the right: **D**-configuration; (+) means dextrorotatory.

sections.heading: 2. Cyclic structures, disaccharides and polysaccharides
sections.body_md:
The open chain does not explain why glucose gives no Schiff’s test or NaHSO₃ adduct, or why the pentaacetate does not react with NH₂OH. Glucose is mainly a **six-membered ring** (pyranose): the C5 –OH adds to the C1 aldehyde (hemiacetal). The two ring forms, **α** (m.p. 419 K) and **β** (m.p. 423 K), differ only at C1 — they are **anomers**. In water each slowly changes to an equilibrium mixture (**mutarotation**). **Fructose** (ketohexose, laevorotatory) forms a five-membered **furanose** ring.

**Glycosidic linkage:** two monosaccharides join with loss of water.
- **Sucrose:** α-D-glucose C1 to β-D-fructose C2 — both reducing carbons used, so **non-reducing**. Hydrolysis changes the rotation from + to − (**invert sugar**).
- **Maltose:** two α-D-glucose, C1–C4 — reducing. **Lactose** (milk sugar): β-D-galactose C1 to glucose C4 — reducing.

**Polysaccharides:** **starch** = amylose (15–20%, unbranched α-1,4, water-soluble, blue with iodine) + amylopectin (80–85%, α-1,4 chains branched by α-1,6 links); **cellulose** = unbranched β-1,4 chains of β-glucose (plant cell walls; humans cannot digest it); **glycogen** = highly branched, animal store in liver and muscle. Each glucose unit in a chain has mass $180 - 18 = 162$.

**Importance:** energy source and store (starch, glycogen), structure (cellulose in wood and cotton), raw material for paper, textiles and ethanol; ribose and deoxyribose in nucleic acids.

The ether (C–O–C) link joining two monosaccharide units, formed with loss of water.
The laevorotatory equimolar mixture of glucose and fructose formed by hydrolysis of dextrorotatory sucrose.

sections.heading: 3. Proteins
sections.body_md:
**α-Amino acids** carry –NH₂ and –COOH on the same carbon, with a side chain R; all except glycine are optically active (L-form in proteins). **Essential** amino acids (e.g. valine, leucine, lysine) must come from food. In water they exist as **zwitterions**, $\ce{H3N+-CHR-COO-}$: amphoteric, crystalline, water-soluble, high-melting.

**Peptide bond:** –COOH of one amino acid + –NH₂ of the next → –CO–NH– + H₂O. A chain of $n$ amino acids has $n - 1$ peptide bonds and is formed with loss of $n - 1$ water molecules. More than about 100 residues: a protein.

**Structure levels:** primary (sequence; covalent peptide bonds), secondary (α-helix or β-pleated sheet; H-bonds between C=O and N–H), tertiary (overall 3D fold; H-bonds, disulfide links, ionic and van der Waals forces), quaternary (arrangement of subunits, e.g. haemoglobin).

**Fibrous** proteins (keratin, myosin): parallel chains, insoluble. **Globular** proteins (insulin, albumin): compact, soluble.

**Denaturation:** heat, pH change or some chemicals disrupt H-bonds and other weak forces, uncoiling secondary and tertiary structure; biological activity is lost but the **primary structure stays**. Examples: boiling an egg, curdling milk.

The amide link –CO–NH– between two amino acids.
Loss of a protein’s secondary and tertiary structure, and of its biological activity, on heating or change of pH.

sections.heading: 4. Enzymes and vitamins
sections.body_md:
**Enzymes** are biocatalysts, almost all globular proteins. They are highly **specific** (one substrate or reaction), work at body temperature and near-neutral pH, and lower the **activation energy**. Examples: invertase (sucrose → glucose + fructose), maltase (maltose → glucose), amylase (starch → maltose), pepsin and trypsin (proteins → peptides), urease (urea → NH₃ + CO₂).

**Vitamins** are organic compounds needed in small amounts for normal growth and health.
- **Fat-soluble:** A, D, E, K — stored in liver and adipose tissue.
- **Water-soluble:** B group and C — excreted in urine, so must be supplied regularly (except B₁₂, stored in the liver). Vitamin C is destroyed by heat.

| Vitamin | Deficiency disease |
|---|---|
| A | Xerophthalmia, night blindness |
| B₁ | Beriberi |
| B₂ | Cheilosis, digestive disorders |
| B₆ | Convulsions |
| B₁₂ | Pernicious anaemia |
| C | Scurvy (bleeding gums) |
| D | Rickets, osteomalacia |
| E | Fragile red blood cells, muscle weakness |
| K | Increased blood-clotting time |

key_terms.definition_md: A biological catalyst, usually a globular protein, that is specific for a reaction and lowers its activation energy.
Vitamins A, D, E and K, which dissolve in fats and are stored in the body.

sections.heading: 5. Nucleic acids and hormones
sections.body_md:
**Nucleic acids** are polymers of **nucleotides**. Nucleoside = base + pentose sugar; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate (at C5′). Nucleotides are joined by **phosphodiester** links (C5′ of one sugar to C3′ of the next).
- **DNA:** 2-deoxy-D-ribose; bases A, G, C, T; **double helix** of two antiparallel complementary strands; A pairs with T (two H-bonds), G with C (three H-bonds), so %A = %T and %G = %C.
- **RNA:** D-ribose; bases A, G, C, **U**; usually single-stranded; three types — mRNA (message), tRNA (carries amino acids), rRNA (in ribosomes).

**Functions:** DNA stores hereditary information and **replicates**; RNA directs **protein synthesis** (transcription to mRNA, translation at ribosomes).

**Hormones** are chemical messengers from endocrine glands, carried in blood: **steroids** (oestrogen, testosterone, glucocorticoids), **polypeptides** (insulin, glucagon), **amino acid derivatives** (adrenaline, thyroxine). Insulin lowers and glucagon raises blood glucose; thyroxine controls metabolic rate (iodine deficiency → goitre, hypothyroidism); adrenaline drives the fight-or-flight response; sex hormones control sexual development.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling sucrose a reducing sugar, or forgetting to explain why it is non-reducing (both anomeric carbons in the glycosidic bond).
- Writing that cellulose is made of α-glucose (it is β-glucose).
- Calling α- and β-glucose enantiomers (they are anomers, differing only at C1).
- Saying denaturation breaks peptide bonds (primary structure is unchanged).
- Putting thymine in RNA or ribose in DNA.
- Listing vitamin C as fat-soluble.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: a name, linkage, vitamin–disease pair or base pair.
- Structure evidence (2–3 marks): reagent, product and the feature it proves.
- Comparisons (2–3 marks): one mark per correct point of difference (DNA/RNA, fibrous/globular, starch/cellulose).
- Calculations: base percentages, number of peptide bonds or water molecules, glucose units in a polysaccharide.

Hydrolysis of sucrose to glucose and fructose.
A, D, E, K.

cards.back_md: B₁: beriberi. C: scurvy. D: rickets.
Nucleoside = base + sugar. Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate.
DNA: deoxyribose; A, G, C, T. RNA: ribose; A, G, C, U.

questions.stem_md: Bromine water oxidises glucose to gluconic acid, which still has six carbon atoms. This shows that glucose contains:

options.text_md: a primary alcohol group at C6

questions.solution_md: A mild oxidant converts –CHO into –COOH without losing carbon; ketones are not oxidised this way — option (a). The –OH count comes from acetylation (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these sugars does not reduce Fehling’s solution?
questions.solution_md: In sucrose both reducing carbons (glucose C1 and fructose C2) are used in the glycosidic bond — option (c). Maltose and lactose keep a free hemiacetal group.

questions.stem_md: Cotton fibre is almost pure cellulose. Cellulose is a polymer of:

options.text_md: α-D-glucose units joined by unbranched C1–C4 links
α-D-glucose units with C1–C6 branch points
β-D-glucose units joined by unbranched C1–C4 glycosidic links
β-D-fructose units joined by C2–C1 links

questions.solution_md: Cellulose is a straight chain of β-glucose with β-1,4 links — option (c). Unbranched α-1,4 chains describe amylose (a); α-1,6 branches occur in amylopectin and glycogen (b).

questions.stem_md: Ribose, C₅H₁₀O₅, a sugar found in RNA, has an aldehyde group in its open-chain form. It is classified as:
questions.solution_md: Aldehyde group → aldose; five carbons → pentose — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Glucose and gluconic acid both give the same dicarboxylic acid when warmed with nitric acid. That acid is:
questions.solution_md: Nitric acid oxidises both the –CHO (or –COOH already present) end and the –CH₂OH end, giving the C₆ dicarboxylic acid, saccharic acid — option (d).

questions.stem_md: α-D-Glucose and β-D-glucose differ in:
questions.solution_md: They are anomers: same ring, same formula, differing only at the anomeric carbon C1 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A solution of cane sugar with a little acid is kept warm in a polarimeter tube for some hours. The observed angle of rotation:
questions.solution_md: Sucrose (+66.5°) hydrolyses to glucose (+52.5°) and fructose (−92.4°); the mixture is laevorotatory, so the sign inverts — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which observation cannot be explained by the open-chain structure of glucose?

options.text_md: Glucose forms an oxime with hydroxylamine
Glucose gives n-hexane on prolonged heating with HI
Glucose does not give Schiff’s test for aldehydes

questions.solution_md: A free –CHO should give Schiff’s test; its absence points to the cyclic hemiacetal form — option (d). The other three fit the open chain.

questions.stem_md: People with lactose intolerance digest milk sugar poorly. Complete hydrolysis of lactose gives:
questions.solution_md: Lactose is β-D-galactose joined to D-glucose — option (b). Glucose + fructose come from sucrose (a) and two glucose from maltose (c).

questions.stem_md: Fructose and glucose have the same molecular formula. Fructose differs because it:

options.text_md: has an aldehyde group and is dextrorotatory
is a disaccharide of two glucose units
has a ketone group at C2 and forms a five-membered ring

questions.solution_md: Fructose is a ketohexose that forms a furanose ring and is laevorotatory; it is still a reducing sugar — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student adds iodine solution to three samples: water in which rice was boiled, wet cotton wool, and a glucose solution. A blue-black colour appears only with:

options.text_md: the cotton wool, because of cellulose
the glucose solution, because glucose is a reducing sugar
the rice water, because of amylose from starch
all three, because all contain glucose units

questions.solution_md: The helical chains of amylose trap iodine, giving the blue-black colour; cellulose and free glucose do not — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Maltose reduces Tollens’ reagent.
questions.solution_md: True. In maltose, C1 of one glucose is joined to C4 of the other, so the second unit keeps a free hemiacetal group that can open to –CHO.

questions.stem_md: True or false? α-D-Glucose and β-D-glucose are a pair of enantiomers.
questions.solution_md: False. They are anomers (diastereomers differing only at C1), not mirror images; their specific rotations are +111° and +19.2°, not equal and opposite.

questions.stem_md: The slow change in the specific rotation of a freshly made solution of α-D-glucose to a steady value is called ___.
questions.solution_md: **Mutarotation**: α and β forms interconvert through the open chain until equilibrium (+52.5°).

questions.stem_md: Match each carbohydrate with the products of its complete hydrolysis.
questions.solution_md: Sucrose → glucose + fructose; maltose → 2 glucose; lactose → galactose + glucose; cellulose → many glucose.

questions.stem_md: Match each reagent with the structural feature of glucose that its reaction with glucose reveals.

match_right.text_md: The carbonyl group is an aldehyde
A –CH₂OH group at the end of the chain
Six carbon atoms in a straight chain

questions.solution_md: HI → n-hexane (straight chain); Br₂ water → gluconic acid (aldehyde); anhydride → pentaacetate (five –OH); HNO₃ → saccharic acid (primary alcohol).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sucrose is a non-reducing sugar.

**Reason (R):** Sucrose is a disaccharide.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but being a disaccharide does not explain it (maltose and lactose are reducing disaccharides). Sucrose is non-reducing because both anomeric carbons form the glycosidic bond — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Humans cannot digest cellulose.

**Reason (R):** Cellulose is a branched polymer of α-D-glucose.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false — cellulose is an unbranched polymer of β-D-glucose, and human enzymes cannot hydrolyse β-1,4 links — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Glucose pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine.

**Reason (R):** In the cyclic form of glucose, C1 is part of a hemiacetal and there is no free aldehyde group.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true; with C1 locked in the ring (and its –OH acetylated), no –CHO is available to form an oxime — option (a).

questions.stem_md: What mass of glucose ($M = 180$), in grams, is formed by complete hydrolysis of $34.2\ \text{g}$ of sucrose ($M = 342$)?
questions.solution_md: $\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O -> C6H12O6 + C6H12O6}$ gives one glucose per sucrose. Moles $= 34.2 \div 342 = 0.1$; mass $= 0.1 \times 180 = 18$, so $18\ \text{g}$.

questions.stem_md: A brewer hydrolyses $17.1\ \text{g}$ of maltose ($M = 342$) completely with the enzyme maltase. What mass of glucose ($M = 180$), in grams, is formed?
questions.solution_md: $\ce{C12H22O11 + H2O -> 2C6H12O6}$: each maltose gives two glucose. Moles of maltose $= 17.1 \div 342 = 0.05$; moles of glucose $= 2 \times 0.05 = 0.1$; mass $= 0.1 \times 180 = 18$, so $18\ \text{g}$.

marking_scheme.step: Two glucose per maltose; 0.1 mol glucose

questions.stem_md: A sample of cotton cellulose has an average molar mass of $4.86 \times 10^{5}\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. How many glucose units does an average chain contain? (Mass of one chain unit, $\ce{C6H10O5}$, $= 162$.)
questions.solution_md: Number of units $= 486000 \div 162 = 3000$.

questions.stem_md: What does each observation tell us about the structure of glucose? (a) Glucose adds HCN to form a cyanohydrin. (b) Warm nitric acid converts glucose into saccharic acid, a six-carbon dicarboxylic acid.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Addition of HCN is a typical reaction of a carbonyl group, so glucose contains a C=O group. (b) Both ends of the chain are oxidised to –COOH without loss of carbon, so besides the aldehyde group, glucose has a primary alcohol group (–CH₂OH) at the other end.

questions.solution_md: Carbonyl group; primary alcohol group.

questions.stem_md: A sweet shop boils cane sugar with water and a little lemon juice to make a syrup. A sample of the syrup gives a red precipitate with Fehling’s solution, but a plain cane sugar solution does not. Explain.

answer.model_answer_md: Cane sugar (sucrose) is non-reducing because both reducing carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond. The acid in lemon juice, on boiling, hydrolyses sucrose into glucose and fructose. These are reducing sugars, so the syrup reduces Fehling’s solution to red Cu₂O.

questions.solution_md: Acid hydrolysis releases reducing sugars.

marking_scheme.step: Acid hydrolysis gives reducing glucose and fructose

questions.stem_md: Rice and cotton are both made mostly of glucose units. Give two structural differences between starch and cellulose that explain why we can digest rice but not cotton.

answer.model_answer_md: Starch is made of α-D-glucose units, while cellulose is made of β-D-glucose units joined by β-1,4 links. Starch is partly branched (amylopectin has α-1,6 branches), whereas cellulose chains are straight and packed tightly by hydrogen bonds into fibres. Our digestive enzymes hydrolyse α-links but not β-links.

questions.solution_md: α vs β glucose; branched vs straight.

marking_scheme.step: α vs β linkage (enzymes hydrolyse only α)

questions.stem_md: Give three observations that the open-chain structure of glucose cannot explain, and explain how the cyclic structure accounts for them.

answer.model_answer_md: Although glucose has an aldehyde group, it does not give Schiff’s test and does not form an addition product with NaHSO₃. Its pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine. Glucose also exists in two crystalline forms, α and β, which show mutarotation in water. In the cyclic structure, the –OH at C5 adds to the C1 aldehyde to form a six-membered hemiacetal ring, so there is little free –CHO. Ring closure makes C1 a new chiral centre, giving the two anomers, which interconvert through the open chain.

questions.solution_md: Schiff’s/NaHSO₃, pentaacetate, α and β forms; hemiacetal ring, anomers.

marking_scheme.step: Hemiacetal ring explains lack of free –CHO

questions.stem_md: A food lab receives four powders: glucose, sucrose, maltose and starch. Predict which give a red precipitate with Fehling’s solution, and explain the basis of your prediction.

answer.model_answer_md: Glucose and maltose give the red precipitate; sucrose and starch do not. A sugar is reducing when it has a free aldehyde or ketone group, or a hemiacetal that can open to one. Glucose is a monosaccharide with such a group, and in maltose the second glucose unit keeps a free hemiacetal at C1. In sucrose both anomeric carbons are joined in the glycosidic bond, and in starch the very few free chain ends are too small a fraction to give a positive test.

questions.solution_md: Glucose and maltose reducing; reason based on free hemiacetal.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe two ways of preparing glucose, with an equation for one.

(b) Describe four reactions of glucose and state what each shows about its open-chain structure.

(c) Explain why glucose is said to have a cyclic structure, and what is meant by α- and β-glucose.

answer.model_answer_md: Glucose is made by boiling sucrose with dilute acid, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ + H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + C₆H₁₂O₆ (fructose), or commercially by hydrolysing starch with dilute H₂SO₄ at 393 K under pressure. Prolonged heating with HI gives n-hexane, so the six carbons form a straight chain. Formation of an oxime shows a carbonyl group. Bromine water gives gluconic acid, so the carbonyl is an aldehyde. Acetylation gives a pentaacetate, so there are five –OH groups. However, glucose gives no Schiff’s test and no NaHSO₃ adduct, because it exists mainly as a six-membered ring formed when the C5 –OH adds to the C1 aldehyde. The two ring forms, α and β, differ only in the position of the –OH at C1; they are anomers.

questions.solution_md: Two preparations; four reactions and inferences; ring closure and anomers.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Evidence for and description of the ring

questions.stem_md:
(a) Classify carbohydrates on the basis of hydrolysis, giving one example of each class.

(b) Explain why sucrose is called non-reducing and why its hydrolysis product is called invert sugar.

(c) Compare amylose, amylopectin, cellulose and glycogen.

answer.model_answer_md: Monosaccharides cannot be hydrolysed further (glucose); oligosaccharides give two to ten units (sucrose, a disaccharide); polysaccharides give many units (starch). In sucrose, C1 of α-glucose is linked to C2 of β-fructose, so neither unit has a free hemiacetal and it cannot reduce Fehling’s or Tollens’ reagent. Sucrose is dextrorotatory, but hydrolysis gives glucose (+52.5°) and fructose (−92.4°); the mixture is laevorotatory, so the sign is inverted. Amylose is an unbranched, water-soluble chain of α-glucose (α-1,4). Amylopectin has α-1,4 chains branched by α-1,6 links. Glycogen is similar but more highly branched and is the animal store. Cellulose is an unbranched chain of β-glucose (β-1,4) that forms plant cell walls.

questions.solution_md: Three classes; sucrose non-reducing and inversion; four polysaccharides.

questions.stem_md: When an egg is boiled, its albumin is denatured. Which level of protein structure remains intact?
questions.solution_md: Heat breaks hydrogen bonds and other weak forces but not the covalent peptide bonds, so the amino acid sequence survives — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Amino acids are crystalline solids with high melting points that dissolve in water but not in benzene. The best explanation is that they:

options.text_md: are large polymers held by peptide bonds
exist as dipolar ions (zwitterions) with strong ionic attractions

questions.solution_md: H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻ behaves like a salt: high melting point, soluble in polar water, insoluble in non-polar solvents — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A hexapeptide is made from six amino acid units. How many peptide bonds does it contain?
questions.solution_md: A linear chain of n units has n − 1 links: 6 − 1 = 5 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The α-helix and the β-pleated sheet are held in shape mainly by:

options.text_md: disulfide bonds between cysteine units only
hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups of the backbone

questions.solution_md: Secondary structure is maintained by backbone C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a fibrous protein?
questions.solution_md: Keratin (hair, nails) has long parallel chains and is insoluble — option (c). The others are globular.

questions.stem_md: Paneer is made by adding lemon juice to hot milk. The milk protein separates as a solid mainly because:

options.text_md: lemon juice hydrolyses the protein into free amino acids
the heat and lower pH denature the protein, which coagulates
citric acid joins lactose units into a polysaccharide
vitamin C in the juice oxidises the peptide bonds

questions.solution_md: Acid and heat disrupt the weak forces holding the protein’s shape; the unfolded chains clump together — option (b). Peptide bonds are not broken (a).

questions.stem_md: Using one glycine and one alanine molecule each time, how many different dipeptides can be formed?
questions.solution_md: The free –NH₂ end can be either residue: Gly–Ala and Ala–Gly are different compounds — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Denaturation of a protein by heat changes the order of its amino acids.
questions.solution_md: False. Denaturation breaks only weak interactions (hydrogen bonds, ionic and van der Waals forces); the peptide bonds and the amino acid sequence are unchanged.

questions.stem_md: The amide link, –CO–NH–, formed between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another is called a ___ bond.
questions.solution_md: A **peptide** bond, formed with loss of water.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Amino acids have high melting points compared with organic compounds of similar molar mass.

**Reason (R):** In the solid, amino acids exist as zwitterions held by strong electrostatic attractions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the salt-like ionic lattice explains the high melting points — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Denaturation of a protein changes its amino acid sequence.

**Reason (R):** Denaturation disrupts the hydrogen bonds that hold the secondary structure of a protein.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false (the primary structure is unchanged); R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: What is the molar mass, in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$, of the dipeptide formed from glycine ($M = 75$) and alanine ($M = 89$)? ($\ce{H2O}$: $M = 18$)
questions.solution_md: One water molecule is lost: $75 + 89 - 18 = 146$, so $146\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between fibrous and globular proteins, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: In fibrous proteins the polypeptide chains run parallel and are held together by hydrogen and disulfide bonds, forming fibres that are insoluble in water, e.g. keratin. In globular proteins the chains coil into compact, roughly spherical shapes that are usually soluble in water, e.g. insulin or albumin.

questions.solution_md: Parallel insoluble fibres vs compact soluble shapes.

questions.stem_md: Explain what happens to the protein when egg white is boiled, and why boiled egg white does not become clear and runny again on cooling.

answer.model_answer_md: Heat breaks the hydrogen bonds and other weak forces that hold the globular albumin in its folded shape, so the chains unfold (denaturation) and tangle together, forming a white solid. On cooling, the randomly tangled chains cannot find their way back to the original folded shape, so the change is not reversed.

questions.solution_md: Denaturation and coagulation; irreversible.

marking_scheme.step: Chains tangle; original shape not regained

questions.stem_md: Describe the primary, secondary and tertiary structures of a protein, naming the bonds or forces that hold each.

answer.model_answer_md: The primary structure is the sequence of amino acids in the chain, held by covalent peptide bonds; a change in a single amino acid can alter the protein’s function. The secondary structure is the regular local folding of the chain into an α-helix or a β-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole chain, held by hydrogen bonds, disulfide bridges, ionic attractions and van der Waals forces between side chains.

questions.solution_md: Three levels with bonds.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain why amino acids behave as salts and are amphoteric.

(b) Show how two amino acids form a dipeptide, and find how many peptide bonds and water molecules are involved in forming a chain of 20 amino acids.

(c) Explain the quaternary structure of a protein and what happens on denaturation.

answer.model_answer_md: In an amino acid the –COOH group gives a proton to the –NH₂ group, forming a zwitterion, H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻. This dipolar ion gives salt-like properties: high melting point and solubility in water. It is amphoteric because –NH₃⁺ can donate a proton to a base and –COO⁻ can accept one from an acid. The –COOH of one amino acid condenses with the –NH₂ of another, losing water and forming a –CO–NH– peptide bond. A chain of 20 amino acids has 19 peptide bonds, formed with loss of 19 water molecules. Quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits, as in haemoglobin. Denaturation by heat or pH breaks weak forces, destroying secondary to quaternary structure and activity, but not the primary structure.

questions.solution_md: Zwitterion; peptide bond with 19 and 19; quaternary; denaturation.

questions.stem_md: A cell needs to make the protein insulin. Describe the roles of DNA, messenger RNA and transfer RNA in this process.

answer.model_answer_md: The gene for insulin is a sequence of bases in DNA, which carries the hereditary instructions. In transcription, the base sequence of this gene is copied into a molecule of messenger RNA, which leaves the nucleus and binds to a ribosome. At the ribosome, transfer RNA molecules each bring a specific amino acid and pair with the matching codon on the mRNA, so the amino acids are lined up in the order set by the gene and joined by peptide bonds.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What are the three components of a nucleotide, and how are nucleotides joined in a nucleic acid?

(b) Describe the double-helix structure of DNA and the base-pairing rules.

(c) A DNA sample contains 26% thymine. Find the percentages of the other bases, and explain why such a calculation is not possible for single-stranded RNA.

answer.model_answer_md: A nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group; base + sugar alone is a nucleoside. Nucleotides are joined by phosphodiester links between C5′ of one sugar and C3′ of the next, forming a sugar–phosphate backbone. DNA has two antiparallel strands coiled into a double helix, with the bases pointing inwards. Adenine pairs with thymine by two hydrogen bonds and guanine with cytosine by three, so the strands are complementary. If T = 26%, then A = 26%, A + T = 52%, G + C = 48% and G = C = 24%. RNA is usually single-stranded, so its bases are not paired one to one and the amounts need not be equal.

questions.solution_md: Three components and linkage; double helix and pairing; 26, 24, 24; single strand.

answer.model_answer_md:

**(b)** 90 g

**(c)** (i) Specificity and mild conditions.

questions.passage_md: A forensic science laboratory extracts DNA from a small blood sample. Before analysis, the double-stranded DNA is heated to about 95 °C so that the two strands separate; on slow cooling they pair up again. A technician reports that the sample contains 22% cytosine. The laboratory also notes that heating at 95 °C does not break the DNA into separate nucleotides.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (a) Cytosine

**(b)** 28 %

**(c)** (i) The two strands are held together only by hydrogen bonds between base pairs, which are weak and break on heating. Within each strand, nucleotides are joined by covalent phosphodiester bonds in the sugar–phosphate backbone, which are much stronger and are not broken at this temperature.

**OR** (ii) The strands are complementary: each A on one strand faces a T on the other and each G faces a C. On slow cooling, the bases can find their partners, and the correct pairing gives the greatest number of hydrogen bonds, so the original double helix reforms.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** G pairs with C by three hydrogen bonds — option (a).

**(b)** G = C = 22%, so G + C $= 44\%$; A + T $= 100 - 44 = 56\%$; A $= 56 \div 2 = 28$, so 28%.

**(c)** (i) Hydrogen bonds vs covalent phosphodiester bonds.

(ii) Complementary base pairing.
